name: flat ground
why: the simplest possible route

name: one step up
why: the game steps up a single tile for free, so it is a walk and not a jump. This grid used to put the goal a row *below* the start, which tested stepping down under the name of stepping up

name: one step down
why: walking off a one-tile ledge

name: goal is where we stand
why: an empty route is arrival, not failure, and Pilot read the two as one

name: two-row tunnel is too short
why: 42 pixels of body will not fit in 32 pixels of gap. The way through is over the wall and down the far side. No blocks are named because no particular block has to go: the wall can be crossed anywhere along it, and pinning cells here would assert which route was chosen rather than that the route is sound. Where the shape is the point, the geometry forces it. See the three cases below

name: three-row tunnel fits
why: 48 pixels of gap is enough

name: one-wide slot is not standable
why: 20 pixels of body cannot sit in a 16 pixel column, so both columns of the wall come out, over all three rows the body occupies. Six blocks. Asserting only that it dug would have passed a route that cut one column and left a slot the character cannot enter

name: jump to a ledge
why: two tiles up is past what a free step-up covers, so this one really does jump. The grid it replaces had the goal a row below the start and never jumped at all

name: a four-tile ledge is jumped, not pillared
why: four tiles used to be out of reach and this scenario used to spend blocks on it, because the jump was hard-coded at three. Measured from the game (jumpSpeed held for jumpHeight frames, then coasting against gravity) it is closer to six, so a four-tile ledge is a hop. Placing a block to reach something you can jump to is time and stone spent on nothing

name: pillar up to a plateau
why: eight rows, which is past what a jump reaches even measured generously, and a face of rock too tall to stair up cheaply. Blocks are the answer here and only here. The four-tile ledge above is a hop, and this scenario had to grow when the jump height was corrected, because at four rows it had stopped testing pillaring at all

name: drop into a two-wide shaft
why: the body fits, so it may fall

name: a one-wide hole is widened, not refused
why: sixteen pixels for a twenty pixel body, so it cannot be dropped into however deep it goes, but the column beside a crack is ordinary rock, and four blocks turn a crack into a shaft. Refusing was right and stopping there was not: it walked away from a goal four swings beneath it. Ebonstone on the far side settles which way it widens, so the scenario names one answer and gets it for a reason. There used to be a parity rule for that, which the follower had to reproduce exactly and did not; a footing names both its columns, so the plan simply says

name: walking beats digging
why: the whole reason mining is an edge and not a rule

name: dig down to a buried goal
why: nothing else will reach it. Which column the shaft goes down is the search's business; that it is two columns wide is asserted where the geometry forces one answer

name: fall down a shaft rather than digging beside it
why: the half of run 09:38 that was never in doubt. Two columns wide, which is what the body is, so the drop is free and no route should pay to dig beside it. Here because the one-wide case below looks like this one from across the room, and the difference between them is a single column

name: dig straight down rather than sideways
why: sealed in rock with the goal directly below. Run 09:38 wandered three columns sideways over two rows before settling into a straight shaft, which a fall priced by how far down it reaches would reward. It does not happen here, so that wander came from the ground and not from the pricing. The step cap holds it: straight down is one step a row

name: a deep one-wide hole is widened all the way down
why: what run 09:38 actually found, and it looks like digging beside the hole because that is what it is. Sixteen pixels for a twenty pixel body, so a one-wide shaft cannot be dropped into however deep it goes, and the column beside it is ordinary rock. The route goes down the hole taking out its neighbour as it goes, one tile a row, which is the one tile a row that run broke for forty rows. Ebonstone on the far side settles which way it widens, so the answer is one shape

name: the shaft beside the dig
why: copied out of a world at (2052, 204), with the body put back where the route was planned from rather than where it had walked to when the copy was taken. The run went west along the surface and then dug column 2058 for fifty rows, with an open two column shaft at 2059 and 2060 beside it the whole way down. A footing on the shaft costs nothing and a footing one column left breaks a tile every row. Cut off at the shaft's known end and floored there, since below that the world is fog and the real goal was seventy rows further down

name: a tree is gone round, not through
why: run 17:34: twenty-two seconds swinging at a tile the game refuses. The pocket is ordinary rock on every side and the floor is protected, so the only descent there is cannot be made, which is the point, since the refusal is silent in game and looks exactly like slow mining. So the route leaves by the side instead, and the invariant that no route may plan to break what the pickaxe cannot is what actually holds it, for every case here rather than only this one. It expected None before, on a grid whose goal sat under a ceiling: refused for being unstandable, with the tree never tested at all

name: too hard for this pickaxe
why: Ebonstone wants 65 and copper is 35. Progression expressed as physics: the corruption is shut until the agent has been to a boss and back, and the search should see a wall rather than carry that rule separately

name: go round the hard rock
why: a wall is only a wall if there is no way past it

name: a shaft is two columns wide
why: the excavation, not merely that one happened. Cutting one column of a two column shaft is still mining, and leaves a hole the body cannot enter, which is the bug this shape came from

name: a sideways tunnel is three rows tall
why: the body is three rows, so a tunnel cut two rows high is one the character cannot walk down. The planner costed exactly that for weeks

name: do not walk into fog
why: unknown is not empty, and it is not a wall to cut either. The agent may not stroll onto fog and no longer tunnels through it, so a goal with nothing but fog in front of it has no route at all. In a world the body walks to the edge of what it knows, which lights one more cell, and the next plan starts from there

name: known ground beats a foggy shortcut
why: the long way round is on the map; the short way is a guess. Fog costs 1.5x precisely so that a seen route wins when there is one

name: go round the pond
why: water halves running speed and the agent has no swimming to speak of, so a pool is somewhere it wallows rather than crosses, which is how a run got spent in one. Eight wet steps along the bottom against one wet step and a dry ledge: the ledge should win by a distance

name: wade when there is no dry way
why: priced, not forbidden. A cost that cannot be paid is a wall, and the way through is sometimes simply wet

name: sealed behind unbreakable rock
why: no route is the correct answer, and saying so beats inventing one

name: walk up a mountain
why: this should work as the agent walks up the mountain

name: climb out with blocks in hand
why: up five and across nine, carrying stone. This used to be called excavate stair and expected one, which was the right answer only while pillaring could not cut its own ceiling: a staircase is five blocks a row and a pillar is two, so the cheap climb is a mix, and it is what a player does. See the buried goal below for the empty-handed version

name: a natural staircase up
why: one-tile terraces. The game steps up each of these for free, so a hill made of them is a walk from bottom to top

name: a natural staircase down
why: the same hill from the top. Falling a tile at a time costs nothing and should not be mistaken for needing a jump

name: a two-tile ledge needs a jump
why: one tile is a free step and two is not, which is the whole difference between the terraces above and this

name: jump to platforms
why: the agent must jump to reach the platforms above

name: fall into a pit
why: four rows is well inside what the planner will fall through, and gravity does the work

name: cut through a thin wall
why: one column thick, three rows of body: three blocks. Going over the top costs more, which is the point of pricing mining by the tile

name: must mine one block
why: the planner must mine one block to proceed, as the gap is not sufficient for passage

name: sink a shaft to a deep goal
why: straight down through solid rock, two columns wide the whole way, because a one-wide shaft is a hole the body cannot enter

name: drop down a long chimney
why: seven rows is inside the fall limit, and a two-wide chimney is one the body fits down

name: stair up to a buried goal
why: a goal above, in rock that can be cut, and nothing to build with. Cutting upward is the expensive way and the agent has to have it: with stone in the bag it pillars instead, correctly, because a placement costs forty ticks and a row of staircase costs five blocks at two hundred. Empty handed is the only way to ask the question this case is named after

name: walk along half blocks
why: a floor of half blocks is a floor. Reading them as walls makes the row above one unusable, so the body has nowhere to be and the flattest ground in the world becomes impassable

name: up a smoothed hillside
why: a hillside as worldgen actually leaves it. One slope per change of height and flat ground between. A row of them side by side would be a sawtooth, which is not a shape any world contains

name: shaped ground sitting on rock
why: half blocks laid over solid stone, which is what a floor looks like almost everywhere. Both rows hold the character up and only the upper one is where it can actually stand. A plan that picks the lower one leaves the step nowhere to go, and the character waits out the stall guard against every shaped tile it meets

name: down a smoothed hillside
why: the same hill descending, which is drawn with the other slope because that is the way it faces. A picture of a hill with its ramps back to front is worse than no picture in a suite whose whole subject is reading shapes

name: a long rolling surface
why: up and down twice over twenty-four columns, with a single slope at each change of height and half blocks along the tops. Long enough that a freeze anywhere on it shows up, and the arena fails a scenario that stands still on a move with nothing to dig

name: the surface it got stuck on
why: copied off a live run, from the terrain dump taken where the agent stood for six seconds: forest floor with tree bases in it, a half block at the far end and a one-tile gap beside it. The gap is narrower than the body and the half block is a floor, so this is a walk from end to end. The run's actual fault was elsewhere (it was searching for wood still falling through the air) but ground the agent has really been stuck on is worth keeping whatever stopped it there

name: dig down through a half block
why: shaped rock is still rock. It reads as a platform because the body fits in the empty part, and a descent that would not break it is a descent sealed by every smoothed floor in the world

name: skirt a deep pool
why: four times the cost per tile means a dry way round wins whenever there is one, even a longer one

name: walk round a patch of fog
why: unknown ground is not walkable, and it is not a wall either. Known ground beside it is simply cheaper

name: tunnel into the unknown
why: it used to. Cutting into fog was how a run reached fifty rows into a pool it could not see, drowned its own light and stood swinging at water, since an unseen cell reports no water and prices as cheap. A swing at unseen air breaks nothing and reveals nothing, so the follower waits for a cell to go that was never there. Now the plan stops at the edge of the known and the digging happens a plan at a time

name: walk round the ebonstone
why: sixty-five against thirty-five. A copper pick makes corruption a wall, and a wall with a way round it is only a detour

name: find the soft seam
why: one pair of ordinary columns in a floor of ebonstone. Everything else underfoot is beyond a copper pick, so the whole scenario is whether the search walks to the two tiles it can actually break instead of standing on the ones it cannot

name: a ledge at exactly the jump's height
why: six tiles, which is what a character clears with no equipment and no buffs: jumpSpeed held for jumpHeight frames, then coasting against gravity, floored. Nothing should be spent getting up here

name: a ledge one tile past the jump
why: seven, which is one more than a jump reaches, and a face of ebonstone so there is no staircase to cut. Blocks are the only way up. This and the six-tile ledge above pin the boundary from both sides: get the height wrong in either direction and exactly one of them fails

name: a one-tile lip on the way
why: a bump in the floor is not an obstacle, and treating it as one is how a follower ends up jumping at every pebble

name: get to the surface
why: the player must build a path to reach the surface from the starting point

name: do a small jump
why: the player must perform a jump to reach the goal

name: jump a gap under a low ceiling
why: the player must cross a gap with rock close overhead

name: build horizontally to do a jump
why: the player must build horizontally to create a path for a jump

name: walk through a work bench
why: the player must pass a crafting station without breaking or climbing it

name: step over what a jump would land on
why: the player must walk over the half block rather than leap past it

name: a six-tile jump onto a ledge one column over
why: copied from a fresh world where the run spent ninety seconds here: the body stands on a one-wide pillar with its right half over air, and the search asks for a jump of the full six tiles that also steps one column left onto a ledge against a wall. The follower pressed left and jump, drifted off the pillar, was replanned back onto it, and never left the ground

name: a six-tile jump onto a ledge, walking in from the right
why: the same ledge, reached the way the run reached it: walking left along the top and stopping on the takeoff column with leftward momentum, then a jump whose heading is also left. The follower pressed left with the jump from the first frame, slid a column past the takeoff before it launched, jumped straight up into the underside of the ledge and fell, every half second for as long as the run lasted

name: a four-tile jump under an overhanging ledge
why: copied from a fresh world where the run spent five minutes here. The ledge overhangs the column left of the pillar the body stands on, so a jump that drifts left from the first frame puts its head under the ledge, one row up, and falls. Rising in the takeoff column and stepping over at the top is the only way up, and it is what the search's arc assumed

name: step down a slope to the left
why: copied from a fresh world where the run skipped wood eleven times in a row: a wood drop and a tree lay to the left, past a slope that runs down one row, and the search found no route to either from three tiles away

name: pillar out of a pool from a slope
why: copied from a fresh world: standing on a slope at the bottom of a pool, sunk half a tile into it, the body overlaps the cell beside its feet, so a bridge block there is refused by the game; and a jump in water does not rise the twenty-four pixels a pillar under the feet needs, so the pillar is never placed. The rim is out of jumping reach from the floor, so the way up is to pillar through the water and jump the last of it

name: six up and five across is not a jump
why: copied from a fresh world: from the top of a one-wide column the search planned a jump six rows up and five columns across to a ledge, which no standing start can make. The body rose, came down on the floor, and the same route was drawn from there sixty times. Height and reach trade off, and with no blocks and unbreakable rock there is no way up

name: six rows from water is not a jump
why: copied from a fresh world, the run that made the first iron pickaxe: standing in a pool, the search planned a six-row jump to the ledge beside it, the wet body could not make it, the edge was refused, the footing wobbled a column and the same jump was planned again for as long as the run lasted. A wet body's jump is a hop of two rows at most, and with no blocks and no dry ground clear of the ledge there is no way up

name: a shaft that bottoms out in fog is still fallen down
why: run 09:38 and again at 10:42, in a real world: fifty rows dug in the column beside an open two column shaft. Supported asked whether the landing had a floor without trusting fog, while the fall that picked that landing had trusted it, so every drop into a shaft was struck out and the only descent left was one that makes its own floor each row. The cap costs one break to get in and the shaft is thirty rows, past the twenty a descent that breaks something may plan, so nothing but a free drop reaches the bottom

name: pillar through a plant by breaking it
why: pillar up to a plateau with sunflowers lying along the first row the tower has to put a block in. A plant neither holds the body up nor blocks it, so every move walks through one and nothing books it to be broken, while the cell still reads as somewhere a block could go, and Terraria then refuses in silence: a run laid wood at one four times a second until it was killed. Breaking it is a swing, so the answer is to book it rather than route round. The plants are not in the way of the body, only of the block, which is why they lie across the row the tower starts from rather than the row it climbs past

name: pillar out of a pool into a chimney
why: copied from the run of 2026-09-12 at 17:25, which got stuck here. Standing in water with rock either side, the way up is three blocks and then two hops. The rock at the head of the left column is the tile being landed on, so the last hop has to go up the open pair of columns to the right of it and come down on top of it: jumped from the column below that rock instead, the body rises one row and hits it
